However, the material is distributed without any warranty, either express or implied. The responsibility for interpretation and use of the material lies with the reader. After the conclusion of pilot tests conducted in 2007 and 2008, a revised version of these guidelines will be published. In the event of new epidemics or pandemics, additional recommendations will be provided. The purpose of this document is to offer infection control guidance to prevent the transmission of acute infectious respiratory diseases in healthcare settings, with a focus on diseases that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern, as defined by the International Health Regulations (2005). Healthcare facility managers may also use this guidance to prepare for epidemics and pandemics. This document is intended for use by government planners, healthcare facility administrators, infection control professionals, occupational health specialists, and other professionals involved in patient care. The infection control advice provided in these guidelines is based on available information about the main routes of pathogen transmission and aims to guide continuous and sustainable improvements in healthcare safety. These guidelines are designed to offer Member States a conceptual framework for adaptation according to local regulations, settings, needs, and resources. Healthcare facilities are encouraged to review and adapt the recommendations accordingly. The guidelines were developed following a systematic review of scientific literature identified through PubMed and the Cochrane Library, as well as secondary papers in multiple languages. International and national infection control guidelines and textbooks were also consulted. The document underwent internal and external peer reviews. The Guideline Steering Group evaluated reviewers' comments, provided guidance when opinions differed, and oversaw the incorporation of amendments and finalization of the document. Pilot tests of the guidelines were conducted in 2007 and 2008 across WHO regions to provide local data on the document's clarity, resource requirements, feasibility, and validity of the interventions. These tests also informed implementation and dissemination strategies. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated after the pilot tests. As knowledge about respiratory disease transmission evolves rapidly, case surveillance and investigations will continue to inform infection control recommendations. Modifications to the guidelines will be made as new information becomes available. Acute respiratory diseases (ARDs) are defined as illnesses of the upper or lower respiratory tract caused by infectious agents transmitted from person to person. Symptoms typically develop rapidly, including fever, cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, shortness of breath, wheezing, or difficulty breathing. Examples of pathogens causing ARDs include rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV), and influenza virus. An adequately ventilated single room is defined as a room with at least 12 air changes per hour (ACH) without controlled air direction. Airborne precaution rooms, used to contain airborne infections, must have at least 12 ACH and controlled air direction. Natural ventilation should direct airflow to areas free of transit or allow rapid dilution of contaminated air into surrounding areas and open air. Airborne transmission refers to the spread of infectious agents via droplet nuclei that remain infectious when suspended in the air over long distances and time. This can be categorized into obligate or preferential airborne transmission. Obligate airborne transmission occurs only through droplet nuclei deposition under natural conditions (e.g., pulmonary tuberculosis), while preferential airborne transmission occurs through multiple routes but predominantly via droplet nuclei (e.g., measles, chickenpox). Hand hygiene is a critical component of infection prevention and control, encompassing handwashing, antiseptic handwashing, antiseptic hand rubbing, or surgical hand antisepsis. The document is divided into six parts: definitions of terms, a summary of recommendations, an introduction to key concepts, detailed infection control recommendations, principles of environmental ventilation, and components of healthcare facility preparedness plans. Annexes provide background information for the recommendations. Standard precautions, including hand hygiene, use of personal protective equipment (PPE), prevention of needle stick injuries, and environmental cleaning, should be routinely applied in all healthcare settings. If these basic precautions are not in place, additional specific precautions will not be effective. Leadership, adequate staffing, education, and engineering controls are fundamental to constructing an effective infection control structure.
